extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and students of story/screenwriting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing, mastering, and innovating film genres and on revealing true character through dramatic choice; includes practical study steps, marketing/positioning advice, and prescriptions for genre-specific conventions. Geared to writing for film (screenplays) broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of history as anachronism
rubrics_metrics.description: The best use of history, and the only legitimate excuse to set a film in the past ... is anachronism — to use the past as a clear glass through which you show us the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting a film in the past, ensure the historic setting illuminates contemporary themes or controversies that are difficult to dramatize directly today. Historical distance should make present dilemmas clear and bearable (examples: GLORY, MICHAEL COLLINS, UNFORGIVEN). Avoid pure chronicle or period detail for its own sake; the past must comment on the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biography must interpret facts as fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: BIOGRAPHY ... must never become a simple chronicle. The biographer must interpret facts as if they were fiction, find the meaning of the subject's life, and then cast him as the protagonist of his life's genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A biographical screenplay should shape real events into a coherent dramatic arc and identify the subject's life-genre (e.g., Courtroom Drama, Modern Epic, Disillusionment Plot). Avoid listing events; instead choose and arrange facts to reveal dramatic meaning and protagonist function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiography requires genuine self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Autobiographical films often lack the very virtue they promise: self-knowledge. For while it's true that the unexamined life is not worth living, it's also the case that the unlived life isn't worth examining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing autobiographically, ensure you have lived experience and insight to justify dramatization; mere life-events without examined meaning produce weak autobiographical films (example: BIG WEDNESDAY). Self-knowledge must be dramatized, not asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docu-drama centers on recent events and must balance drama/documentary value
rubrics_metrics.description: DOCU-DRAMA centers on recent rather than past events. Once invigorated by cinema verité ... it's become a popular TV genre, sometimes powerful, but often with little documentary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using docu-drama techniques, preserve documentary credibility where appropriate; beware of converting recent facts into pure melodrama that loses documentary worth. Decide the balance between factual integrity and dramatic shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mockumentary uses documentary form to satirize institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: This genre pretends to be rooted in actuality or memory, behaves like documentary or autobiography, but is utter fiction. It subverts fact-based filmmaking to satirize hypocritical institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing a mockumentary, adopt documentary conventions convincingly (interviews, archival style, observational footage) and use that authenticity to expose and satirize target institutions or social mores (examples: THIS IS SPINAL TAP; ZELIG). Maintain the pretense of actuality for maximal satirical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical's reality permits singing and dancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Descended from opera, this genre presents a 'reality' in which characters sing and dance their stories. It's often a Love Story, but it can be Film Noir, Social Drama, Punitive Plot, Biography, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and honor the internal logic that characters express emotion and plot through song and dance. Any core genre can be adapted to musical form; ensure transitions into musical expression feel truthful to the story-world (examples: SUNSET BOULEVARD, WEST SIDE STORY, ALL THAT JAZZ, EVITA). Musical comedy may satirize other genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fiction as a setting for core genres
rubrics_metrics.description: In hypothetical futures ... the SCIENCE FICTION writer often marries the man-against-state Modern Epic with Action/Adventure. But, like history, the future is a setting in which any genre may play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speculative or future settings to externalize or intensify the central human conflicts of whatever core genre you are working in (e.g., use sci‑fi to enact Disillusionment Plot inner conflicts as in SOLARIS). Don't let spectacle substitute for the genre's essential value conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports genre as crucible for character change
rubrics_metrics.description: Sport is a crucible for character change. This genre is a natural home for the Maturation Plot, Redemption Plot, Education Plot, Punitive Plot, Testing Plot, Disillusionment Plot, Buddy Salvation, Social Drama, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a sports film, make the sport the testing ground for the protagonist's inner growth and values; align the gameplay and competition with the chosen plot archetype (examples: NORTH DALLAS FORTY; RAGING BULL; CHARIOTS OF FIRE; THE LION KING). Use sport-specific scenes to dramatize stakes and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy and animation allow bending of physical laws but must serve genre values
rubrics_metrics.description: FANTASY ... bending and mixing the laws of nature and the supernatural. ANIMATION: Anything can become something else; law of universal metamorphism rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extra-reality deliberately to explore genre themes; although fantasy/animation permit imaginative freedoms, they should still be harnessed to the story's emotional and value architecture. Consider audience expectations (animation skews youthful but can be adult) and genre crossovers (fantasy with love, political allegory, maturation plots, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Film conventions: unconventionality and cerebral mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The ART FILM ... primary internal conventions are, first, a celebration of the cerebral; the Art Film favors the intellect by smothering strong emotion under a blanket of mood ... Secondly and essentially, the story design of an Art Film depends on one grand convention: unconventionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing an Art Film (including Minimalism or Antistructure), cultivate ambiguity, symbolism, mood, and interpretive invitation; external conventions (absence of stars, indie production, foreign language) often accompany marketing. Expect critical rather than mass-audience positioning and aim for formal unconventionality as a deliberate tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and research your genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Each writer's homework is first to identify his genre, then research its governing practices. You must not only respect but master your genre and its conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume familiarity from casual viewing. Study both successes and failures in your genre, rent films, buy screenplays, dissect works 'stop and go', breaking them into setting, role, event, and value. Stack analyses to discover the consistent conventions of time/place/character/action you must anticipate and manipulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre determines design and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each genre imposes conventions on story design: conventional value charges at climax ... conventional settings ... events ... roles. The audience knows these conventions and expects to see them fulfilled. Consequently, the choice of genre sharply determines and limits what's possible within a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a genre with clear awareness that it constrains story choices. Anticipate what audiences expect and use those conventions as resources; omitting or misusing conventions will alienate audiences. Align structure, climax, roles, and values to the chosen genre's demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand genre conventions (settings, roles, events, values)
rubrics_metrics.description: GENRE CONVENTIONS are specific settings, roles, events, and values that define individual genres and their subgenres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog the conventions of your genre: what must appear early (e.g., crime must include a crime), what roles are necessary (e.g., detective), what events and value-resolutions are expected (e.g., punishment of criminal in classic crime). Use conventions as a framework; avoid cliche by finding fresh solutions within them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disillusionment Plot conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary convention of the Disillusionment Plot is a protagonist who opens the story filled with optimism ... second convention is a pattern of repeatedly negative story turns ... leaving him deeply cynical and disillusioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a Disillusionment Plot, structure repeated setbacks that progressively erode the protagonist's idealism, ensuring the arc culminates in a transformed, disillusioned worldview. Use varied, credible pathways to hopelessness to keep the form rich and avoid repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime genre rigid requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Crime Genre there must be a crime; it must happen early in the telling. There must be a detective character ... who discovers clues and suspects. Ultimately, the cop must identify, apprehend, and punish the criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing within the Crime Genre, include the crime early, develop investigative plotting, clue discovery, suspecting, and (traditionally) resolution with justice served. If you subvert this (e.g., CHINATOWN), do so knowingly and in cultural context that supports the subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's overriding convention: nobody gets hurt
rubrics_metrics.description: One overriding convention unites this mega-genre and distinguishes it from drama: Nobody gets hurt. In Comedy, the audience must feel that ... it doesn't really hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a safe comedic tone where consequences are reversible or non-lethal; if you intend darker laughs (Black Comedy), manage audience pain so it is sharp but not unbearable. Use tonal control (e.g., A FISH CALLED WANDA preview test showed gore killed the laugh) to preserve comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of genre requires deep, comparative study
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre study is best done in this fashion: First, list all those works you feel are like yours ... rent the films on video and purchase the screenplays ... study the films stop and go, breaking each film down into elements of setting, role, event, and value. Lastly, stack these analyses ... asking: What do the stories in my genre always do?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a disciplined study routine: analyze both successes and failures, compare multiple texts, identify invariant conventions, and use those findings to anticipate audience expectations and innovate responsibly. The study of failures is emphasized as illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning the audience (marketing must match content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positioning the audience means ... We don't want people coming to our work cold and vague ... We want them to settle into their seats, warm and focused with an appetite we intend to satisfy. Skillful marketing creates genre expectation ... Having told our filmgoers to expect a favorite form, we must deliver as promised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure title, poster, ads, and promotion set accurate genre expectations; mispositioning leads to audience confusion and bad word-of-mouth (example: MIKE'S MURDER). Align marketing promises with the story's actual genre and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Limitation: freedom within constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of Creative Limitation calls for freedom within a circle of obstacles. Talent is like a muscle: without something to push against, it atrophies. We deliberately put rocks in our path, barriers that inspire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose deliberate constraints (genre conventions, form rules) to force inventive solutions. Use constraints to stimulate surprising associations and images, but distinguish convention from cliche by seeking fresh ways to fulfill required elements (e.g., reinvent standard hero-at-mercy scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include imperative genre scenes or tests (Action/Adventure example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Action/Adventure one convention: The hero is at the mercy of the villain ... From a position of helplessness, must turn the tables on the villain. This scene is imperative. It tests and expresses in absolute terms the protagonist's ingenuity, strength of will, and cool under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and include genre-defining set-pieces that test the protagonist's qualities. If the set-piece is present but solved in a tired cliche, refresh it with an inventive solution (examples: RAIDERS, DIE HARD). Missing such a scene can leave the audience dissatisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing genres to enrich meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are frequently combined to resonate with meaning, to enrich character, and to create varieties of mood and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subplots and cross-genre elements (e.g., Love Story inside Crime Story) to create layered tones and fresh story types. Command of genre allows you to invent hybrid types that feel new yet grounded in recognizable conventions (example: THE FISHER KING).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinvent genres responsively and knowingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre conventions ... evolve, grow, adapt, modify, and break apace with the changes in society. The finest writers are ... visionary. They ... produce works that break convention and take the genres into their next generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To successfully break or subvert conventions, be attuned to societal shifts that make the subversion meaningful (example: CHINATOWN's down-ending crime story after Watergate/Vietnam). Reinvention should reinterpret core human values for contemporary audiences; otherwise the work risks feeling antique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a sustaining subject/genre (gift of endurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriting is not for sprinters ... a quality screenplay consumes six months, nine months, a year, or more. Ask yourself, therefore, what will keep your desire burning over those many months? ... What's my favorite genre? Then write in the genre you love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects and genres that you can sustain passion for over long development periods. Focused oeuvre and recurring themes (Hemingway, Dickens) provide longevity; avoid writing for perceived social importance or critical approval if it won't sustain your commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character vs. characterization: reveal true character through choice under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: CHARACTERIZATION is the sum of all observable qualities ... but it is not character. TRUE CHARACTER is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure — the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between surface traits (appearance, speech, habits) and the inner, moral/psychic essence revealed by decisions under pressure. Structure scenes that force crucial choices so the protagonist's true nature is dramatized rather than described.
